topics.desc: Many mountains form when Earth's plates push together and the crust folds or lifts, or when volcanoes build cones, or when a fault lifts a block of crust. Water and ice then wear them down. A mountain range can take a very long time to build. The Rockies, the Himalayas, and volcanic peaks don't all have the exact same story, but they share those big ideas.

topics.title: The Middle Ages
topics.desc: The Middle Ages, or medieval period, is a long stretch of European history usually placed between the end of the Western Roman Empire and the start of the early modern era. Life wasn't only knights and castles: most people farmed, and other parts of the world had their own histories at the same time. Dates are a convenience, not a switch that flipped in one year.

topics.title: The French Revolution
topics.desc: The French Revolution, beginning in 1789, was a period when France's monarchy was overthrown and the country went through deep, often violent political change, with ideas about rights, citizenship, and power still discussed today. It wasn't a single event. Causes included money troubles, inequality, and new political ideas. A class timeline helps more than one slogan.

topics.title: The Enlightenment
topics.desc: The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement, especially in the 1600s and 1700s, that emphasized reason, observation, and debate about government, rights, and knowledge. Thinkers didn't all agree, and not everyone in society gained power at once. Some of those ideas later showed up in documents and revolutions, including in the United States. A class usually names a few people and a few core claims.

topics.title: The printing press
topics.desc: The printing press, developed in Europe in the 1400s by Johannes Gutenberg in a well-known form, made it possible to copy books much faster than by hand. That helped ideas, news, and religious texts spread more widely, though literacy still took time to grow. Printing existed in other forms in other places too; the European press is the usual classroom focus for later European history.

topics.title: The thirteen colonies
topics.desc: The thirteen colonies were British colonies on the Atlantic coast of North America that later became the first U.S. states. They were not all the same: economies, religions, and relations with Native nations differed by region. They existed under British rule before the American Revolution. A map and a regional split, such as New England, the middle colonies, and the South, is the usual class view.

topics.title: Reconstruction
topics.desc: Reconstruction was the period after the U.S. Civil War when the country tried to reunite and to define freedom and rights for formerly enslaved people. There were real gains, then a violent backlash, and many of those gains were rolled back for a long time. It's not only a story of laws on paper. A class usually covers amendments, political conflict, and the end of that era.

topics.title: Women's suffrage
topics.desc: Women's suffrage is the right of women to vote. In the United States, the 19th Amendment in 1920 barred denying the vote on the basis of sex, after a long campaign, but in practice not every woman could vote equally right away because of racism and other barriers. Other countries have their own dates. A class usually covers the movement, not only one year.

topics.title: The Berlin Wall
topics.desc: The Berlin Wall was a barrier built in 1961 by East Germany that divided Berlin during the Cold War, meant to stop people from leaving for the West. It stood until 1989, when it was opened and later torn down, a symbol of the Cold War's end in Europe. Families and a city were split for decades. A map of East and West Berlin helps the story make sense.

topics.title: The United Nations
topics.desc: The United Nations, or UN, is an international organization founded in 1945 after World War II, where member countries discuss peace, development, and other shared problems. It can pass resolutions and run programs, but it doesn't replace a country's government. It isn't a world government. A class usually covers the founding and a few of its bodies, such as the General Assembly.

topics.title: Westward expansion
topics.desc: Westward expansion is the 19th-century movement of the United States' claims and settlers across the continent. It is often told as a pioneer story, but it also involved the displacement, broken treaties, and violence faced by Native nations who already lived on that land, and it included forced migrations such as the Trail of Tears. A fair account holds both the settler story and that cost.

topics.title: Adding fractions
topics.desc: To add fractions, give them a common denominator, add the numerators, and simplify if you can. For 1/4 + 1/2, rewrite 1/2 as 2/4, then add to get 3/4. Mixed numbers can be turned into improper fractions first, or you can add whole numbers and fractions separately with care. Same denominator means you only add the top numbers, not the bottoms.

topics.title: Multiplying fractions
topics.desc: To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators together and the denominators together, then simplify. For 2/3 × 1/4, you get 2/12, which simplifies to 1/6. You can cancel common factors first if that helps. Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes a number smaller, which surprises people who only think of multiplication as making things bigger.

topics.title: Dividing fractions
topics.desc: To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal: flip the second fraction, then multiply. For 1/2 ÷ 1/4, flip 1/4 to 4/1, then multiply to get 2. A common phrase is 'keep, change, flip,' meaning keep the first fraction, change division to multiplication, and flip the second. Check with a simple picture, like how many quarter-pieces fit into a half.

topics.title: Fractions, decimals, and percents
topics.desc: Fractions, decimals, and percents can name the same amount in different forms. 1/2 is 0.5, which is 50 percent. To convert, you use place value and the idea that percent means per 100. Pick the form that makes the problem easier, and double-check by converting back. A simple table of common ones, like 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, is worth knowing.

topics.title: Comparing mean, median, and mode
topics.desc: The mean is the average, the median is the middle value once the numbers are ordered, and the mode is the value that appears most often. A set can have one mode, more than one, or no mode if nothing repeats. Use the one that matches the question: typical average, middle value, or most common category. Outliers pull the mean more than the median.

topics.title: The coordinate plane
topics.desc: The coordinate plane is a grid with a horizontal x-axis and a vertical y-axis that meet at the origin (0, 0). A point is named (x, y): first the left-right value, then the up-down value. The four sections are quadrants. Plotting a few points carefully is the way to get comfortable, and signs tell you which side of the origin you're on.

topics.title: A variable in algebra
topics.desc: In algebra, a variable is a letter that stands for a number, often one you don't know yet, like x in x + 3 = 10. It can also stand for a number that can change in a formula. This is different from a variable in a computer program, even though both are names that hold values. You can do the same operation to both sides of an equation to find what the letter equals.

topics.title: Evaluating an expression
topics.desc: Evaluating an expression means plugging in the given numbers and computing the result, following the order of operations. If x is 3, then 2x + 1 is 2 times 3 plus 1, which is 7. Parentheses, exponents, multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction, still apply. Write the substitution clearly so you don't lose a sign or a product.

topics.title: Two-step equations
topics.desc: A two-step equation needs two inverse operations to isolate the variable, such as 2x + 3 = 11: subtract 3, then divide by 2 to get x = 4. Do the same thing to both sides, and check by plugging the answer back in. It builds on one-step equations. If the variable is in more than one place, that's a different pattern, and you combine like terms first.

topics.title: Finding the whole from a percent
topics.desc: If you know a part and a percent, you can find the whole. If 30 is 25 percent of a number, then the number is 30 divided by 0.25, which is 120. A percent equation, part = percent times whole, is the usual setup. Convert the percent to a decimal first. Check that the part is smaller than the whole when the percent is less than 100.

topics.title: Body paragraphs
topics.desc: A body paragraph in an essay usually has a clear point, evidence or a concrete example, and a sentence that ties it back to your thesis. One main idea per paragraph is easier to follow than a pile of unrelated facts. Transitions help the reader get from one paragraph to the next. If a paragraph is trying to do three jobs, split it.

topics.title: Topic sentences
topics.desc: A topic sentence states the main point of a paragraph, often at the start, so the rest of the paragraph can support it. It should be specific enough to prove, not a vague 'this is important.' If your examples don't match the topic sentence, change one or the other. You can adjust it after you draft if that helps.

topics.title: Writing a hook
topics.desc: A hook is the opening that gets a reader reasonably interested, such as a short surprising fact, a question, or a small scene, then you still have to get to your point. Don't spend the whole introduction on a huge story, and don't use a dictionary definition as a default. A hook should fit the assignment, not only sound flashy.

topics.title: Writing a first draft
topics.desc: A first draft is for getting ideas on the page, not for sounding finished. Use your outline if you have one, skip ahead if a section is stuck, and leave holes you can fill later. You can write a messy version and then revise. Waiting for a perfect first sentence is a common way to write nothing.

topics.title: Email subject lines
topics.desc: A subject line should be short and specific, like 'Question about Friday's homework' rather than 'Hi' or a blank subject. Name the class or the reason if you're writing to a teacher. You'll get a better reply if the person can tell what the email is about before they open it. Don't put the whole message in the subject.

topics.title: Writing a formal email
topics.desc: A formal email has a clear subject, a greeting, a short reason for writing, what you need, and a polite close with your name. Use regular capitalization and complete sentences. This is broader than emailing a teacher, but the same habits help with a coach, a supervisor, or an office. Don't write in all caps, and don't send until you've checked the recipient.

topics.title: A counterargument
topics.desc: A counterargument is a reasonable point someone on the other side might make, which you then answer. Including one can make an essay stronger if you treat it fairly and explain why your claim still holds. Don't invent a silly version of the other side that's easy to knock down. A short, honest objection is enough in many school essays.

topics.title: Integrating a quotation
topics.desc: To integrate a quotation, introduce it with a signal phrase, use only the words you need, and then explain how it supports your point. Don't drop a quote in as its own paragraph with no lead-in. Keep the citation style your class asked for, and quote accurately. A short, well-explained line is better than a long block you never discuss.

topics.title: Starting an essay when you're stuck
topics.desc: If you're stuck starting an essay, write the thesis or a body paragraph first, or type a messy sentence you can fix later. Re-read the prompt and list three points you could actually support. A timer for ten minutes of no-deleting draft can get you moving. You don't have to begin with the introduction just because that's where the reader will start.

topics.title: A thank-you email
topics.desc: A thank-you email is short: say thanks, name the specific thing they did, and add one sincere line if it fits, then close with your name. You don't need a long story. Send it reasonably soon, and keep the tone like you'd speak politely in person. A subject line like 'Thank you for the recommendation' is enough.

topics.title: Feeling sad
topics.desc: Feeling sad is a normal response when something hurts, changes, or doesn't go the way you hoped. You don't have to justify it or cheer up on a schedule. Name it, tell someone you trust if that helps, and do one small kind thing for yourself, like rest or a short walk. If sadness stays heavy for a long time or daily life is hard, that's a reason to talk with a parent, counselor, or another trusted adult. I'm here to listen, not to replace that kind of help.

topics.title: Feeling lonely
topics.desc: Loneliness is the feeling that you want more connection than you have right now, even if people are around. It doesn't mean you're unlikable. One message to a safe person, a shared activity, or being around people without a huge conversation can help a little. If it has lasted and feels heavy, tell a trusted adult. You deserve company that is kind, and it's okay to start small.

topics.title: Feeling nervous
topics.desc: Nerves often show up before something that matters: a test, a talk, or meeting people. Your body can feel jumpy even when you're not in danger. Slow breaths, arriving a little early, and naming what you're going to do first can help. It's okay to be nervous and still go ahead. If nerves are so big you can't do daily things, a trusted adult should hear about it.

topics.title: Feeling angry
topics.desc: Anger is a real feeling, often a sign that something feels unfair, blocked, or hurt. You can feel it without taking it out on someone. Step away if you can, breathe, and name the problem in a sentence once you're cooler. It's okay to say you're mad; it's not okay to hurt people or yourself. If anger feels out of control, that's a reason to get help from a trusted adult.

topics.title: Feeling left out
topics.desc: Feeling left out hurts, and the feeling is valid even if no one meant it that way. You can name it to a trusted friend, make other plans, and you don't have to pretend it doesn't sting. It isn't proof that you're not wanted everywhere. If a group is repeatedly unkind, that's about them, and an adult can help you think about next steps. You still get to belong somewhere.

topics.title: Feeling jealous
topics.desc: Jealousy can show up when someone has a thing, a friendship, or a kind of attention you want. It doesn't make you a bad person. Notice it, avoid taking it out on them, and name what you actually want, which might be something you can work toward or a feeling you can talk about. Comparing every detail of your life to someone else's highlight reel usually makes it worse.

topics.title: Feeling embarrassed
topics.desc: Embarrassment is that hot, exposed feeling after a mistake, a fall, or being called out. It almost always feels bigger to you than it does to everyone else, and most people move on faster than you think. A short recovery, a little humor if it fits, or just going on with your day is enough. You don't have to disappear, and one awkward moment isn't your whole story.

topics.title: Setting a boundary
topics.desc: A boundary is a clear line about what you are and aren't okay with, said as calmly as you can. 'I don't want to talk about that' or 'I can't hang out tonight' are enough. You don't have to give a long speech, and a kind person can respect a no. If someone keeps pushing past a reasonable boundary, tell a trusted adult, especially if you feel unsafe.

topics.title: Saying no
topics.desc: You can say no without a made-up excuse: 'I can't,' 'I don't want to,' or 'not this time' are complete answers. A short, clear no is kinder than a maybe you don't mean. If you feel pressured, repeating the no and leaving the situation is fair. You don't owe anyone your time, your things, or a yes that feels wrong. If the pressure is about safety, get an adult involved.

topics.title: Reaching out when you need support
topics.desc: Reaching out when you need support is a skill, not a failure. Be as specific as you can about what you need, and go to a person who can actually help, like a parent, teacher, counselor, or a friend you trust. You don't have to have the perfect words. If the problem is big, scary, or about your safety, that's exactly when you should tell an adult, even if it feels awkward.

topics.title: A friendship that's changing
topics.desc: Friendships can change when people grow, switch schools, or just want different things. That can feel like a loss even when no one did something cruel. You can talk about it, make a little room, and still be decent. Not every friendship is meant to stay exactly the same. If a change includes being treated badly, you get to step back and talk with a trusted adult.

topics.title: After an argument with a friend
topics.desc: After an argument, give both of you a little time if things are still hot, then talk about the specific thing that happened instead of dragging in every old complaint. A real apology names what you did, if you did something. You can want to stay friends and still need a boundary. If arguments turn into insults or you feel unsafe, get an adult involved.

topics.title: Peer pressure
topics.desc: Peer pressure is when people around you push you toward a choice you wouldn't make on your own, sometimes with jokes, eye rolls, or 'everyone's doing it.' You can say no, leave, or text an adult if you need an out. Your gut is worth listening to, especially if a choice could get someone hurt or in trouble. A real friend can respect a no.

topics.title: Being a good friend
topics.desc: A good friend is reasonably reliable, listens, keeps private things private, and repairs a mistake when they mess up. You don't have to be available every second or agree with everything. Friendship is two-way: you can be kind and still have limits. If a friendship is only taking, or it often leaves you feeling worse, that's worth talking about with someone you trust.

topics.title: Camping basics
topics.desc: Camping goes better with a plan for shelter, weather, water, food that doesn't need a lot of fuss, a light, and a way to tell someone where you'll be. Practice a tent at home if it's new, pack layers, and follow the site's rules. Leave the place as clean as you found it, or better. A first trip can be close to home. I won't invent gear prices; tell me your budget if you're packing a list.

topics.title: Leave no trace
topics.desc: Leave no trace means you pack out what you packed in, stay on trails when that's the rule, leave plants and objects where they are, and keep wildlife wild by not feeding it. It's so the next person, and the place itself, aren't stuck with your mess. Even a little wrapper counts. Local rules at a park or campground still come first.

topics.title: Building a campfire safely
topics.desc: Only build a fire where it's allowed, in a proper ring or pit, away from tents and low branches, with water or dirt ready to put it fully out. An adult should be in charge if you're new or if rules require it. Never use gasoline, and don't leave a fire, even a small one. If the area has a fire ban, skip it. The fire is out only when it's cool to the touch.

topics.title: What to pack for a hike
topics.desc: For a hike, pack water, a layer for weather, a little food, a charged phone, and anything you need for sun or blisters, plus a way to carry trash out. Tell someone your route, and don't pack so much that the bag is miserable. A short hike still needs water. I won't invent prices; tell me the length and weather if you want help thinking through a list.

topics.title: Poison ivy
topics.desc: Poison ivy is a plant that can cause an itchy rash in many people, often with leaves in groups of three, but plants vary, so don't rely on one rhyme alone. Don't touch it, don't burn it, and wash skin and clothes if you think you brushed it. If a rash is serious, near the eyes or mouth, or you're having a strong reaction, get medical help and tell an adult. I'm not a doctor, and a picture from a local guide is better than a guess.

topics.title: Tick checks
topics.desc: After time in grass or woods, check your clothes and skin for ticks, including hidden spots, and have a parent help with places you can't see. Wear longer sleeves or pants if you can, and stay on the path when that's an option. If a tick is attached, an adult should help with safe removal and with any follow-up questions for a doctor. Don't wait and hope if you're unsure.

topics.title: Sportsmanship
topics.desc: Sportsmanship is playing fair, shaking it off after a bad call, and treating the other team and your own as people, not enemies. You can want to win and still be decent. Cheering is fine; mocking is not. After the game, a 'good game' and moving on is enough. If someone is being cruel, you can walk away and tell a coach.

topics.title: Swimming safety
topics.desc: Swim where there's a lifeguard or a responsible adult, and don't dive in water you haven't checked. Know your limits, stay in a buddy system if that's the rule, and get out if you're too cold or too tired. Don't mess around with holding someone under. If someone is in trouble, yell for help rather than becoming a second victim if you're not trained.

topics.title: Fishing basics
topics.desc: Fishing basics are a legal spot, a simple rod, bait or a lure, and patience, plus following local rules about licenses and what you can keep. Handle hooks carefully, and don't leave line behind. If you keep a fish, an adult should help with what's allowed. I won't invent license fees; check local rules, and tell me if you want a simple gear list in a budget.

topics.title: Bike safety on the road
topics.desc: On a road or bike path, wear a helmet, use lights if it's dim, ride with traffic where that's the rule, and signal when you can. Watch for doors, driveways, and wet or icy patches. A sidewalk may or may not be allowed, depending on the place. Make yourself easy to see, and assume a driver might not have seen you yet.

topics.title: Having a catch
topics.desc: Having a catch works better if you agree on a distance, watch the ball into your hands, and don't throw harder than the other person can handle. A glove helps for a baseball; hands can work for a soft ball. Call for the ball if two people might go for it, and stop if something hurts. It's fine to start close and step back as you get the hang of it.

topics.title: Staying found on a trail
topics.desc: Stay found by sticking to the marked trail, telling someone your plan, carrying a charged phone, and turning around early enough that you're not hiking out in the dark. If you think you're off the path, stop, don't wander in bigger circles, and use your map or your phone if you have a signal. A short trail can still get confusing at a fork. Pride is a bad reason to push farther.

topics.title: Trivia
topics.desc: Trivia is a game of short questions and answers, for fun, not a test grade. You can play with cards, an app, or questions you take turns asking. Guessing is allowed, and so is saying you don't know. If you're not sure a fact is true, that's a good moment to check it. Keep the questions kind, and it works as well with two people as with a group.

topics.title: Charades
topics.desc: Charades is a game where you act out a word or a title without talking, and others guess. Agree on categories and a time limit, then keep clues big and simple. No mouthing the words. It's okay if a round is silly or a guess is wrong. A phone timer and a short list of ideas are enough to start.

topics.title: Twenty questions
topics.desc: Twenty questions is a guessing game: one person thinks of something, and others ask yes-or-no questions, usually up to twenty, to figure it out. Start with big categories, like animal, place, or object, then narrow it down. Honest yes-or-no answers keep it fair. If you go past twenty, you can decide whether a guess still counts.

topics.title: Two truths and a lie
topics.desc: Two truths and a lie is a get-to-know-you game: you say three statements, one of them false, and others guess which is the lie. Keep it kind and something you'd be okay sharing, not a trap about someone else. The fun is in a believable mix, not in embarrassing anyone. After people guess, you reveal which one was the lie.

topics.title: I spy
topics.desc: I spy is a simple game: one person says 'I spy, with my eye, something...' and names a color or a clear detail, and others guess the object that's actually in view. Take turns, and pick something people can reasonably see. It's a good waiting game. If a guess is close, you can give a second hint.

topics.title: An indoor treasure hunt
topics.desc: An indoor treasure hunt is a list of things to find or clues to follow inside a house or a classroom, with a clear boundary so no one leaves the area. Write clues that are fair, and keep it safe and kind. A short list is enough for a first hunt. Hide items so they can be found without making a mess you won't put back.

topics.title: Building a blanket fort
topics.desc: A blanket fort is chairs, a couch, or a table with blankets draped over, plus pillows inside. Don't block vents, heaters, or a doorway you need, and keep lights that can get hot out of the blankets. Ask before you take every cushion in the house. When you're done, putting it back is part of the project.

topics.title: Optical illusions
topics.desc: An optical illusion is a picture or scene that tricks your eyes or brain, so you see motion, hidden shapes, or two readings in one image. It's a fun way to notice that seeing is something your brain puts together, not a perfect camera. If you don't see an illusion the way someone else does, that's common. You can look up famous ones; I can also explain how some types work.

topics.title: Why we get brain freeze
topics.desc: Brain freeze is that short, sharp headache some people get after eating or drinking something very cold too quickly. A common explanation is that cold on the roof of the mouth sets off nerves and a quick change in blood vessels, and it usually passes in a short time. Slowing down and warming the roof of your mouth with your tongue can help. If headaches are frequent or severe in general, that's a question for a parent and a doctor.

topics.title: Palindromes
topics.desc: A palindrome is a word, phrase, or number that reads the same forward and backward, like 'level,' 'racecar,' or 121. Spaces and punctuation are often ignored in a phrase. They're just for fun, and you can try making a short one. Not every mirrored-looking word actually qualifies, so check letter by letter.

topics.title: A paper fortune teller
topics.desc: A paper fortune teller, or cootie catcher, is a folded square of paper you open and close with your fingers while someone picks colors or numbers, then a flap reveals a silly message you wrote. Keep the messages kind. Any square paper works, and there are lots of folding guides if the first fold is confusing. It's a classic rainy-day thing, not actual fortune-telling.

topics.title: Making shadow puppets
topics.desc: Shadow puppets are shapes you make with your hands or cut paper in front of a lamp so they show up on a wall. Use a simple light, keep it away from anything that can burn, and leave room so no one bumps the lamp. A bird, a dog, or a talking mouth are classic starts. Dim the room a little so the shadow is clearer.
